newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central Africa mutiny turns into tribal witch-hunt.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa mutiny turns into tribal witch-hunt.

text.p: Supporters of Central African Republic President Ange-Felix Patasse put up roadblocks in their bastions of the capital Bangui on Monday as a two-week army mutiny degenerated into a tribal witch-hunt.
Residents said pro-Patasse militants seized at least four hostages from the Yakoma tribe where most of the mutinous soldiers are drawn.
The abducted people included state television technician Francois Kpakata, who was seized on Monday, they said.
Witnesses said barricades mounted by members of Patasse's Baya tribe went up on Monday in the Combatants area and Sarra. Militants looking for Yakomas checked residents' identities.
At the same time roadblocks appeared on roads leading to rebel strongholds in the south and west of the city.

Residents said Patasse's supporters were trying to pre-empt any attack by mutineers. They said rebels wanted to reach Boyirab district which mutineers say is full of civilians armed by Patasse and "codos" (hired guns) from Chad and Sudan.
Police sources said a Yakoma house was set on fire in Bangui's Quartier Combatants in the 18th Arrondisement.
"The house has been burning since yesterday," one police officer said.

An eight-party opposition alliance began its efforts on Monday to mediate between the government and mutineers after church-brokered talks hit stalemate over rebel demands for Patasse's resignation. The president has dismissed this.
Alliance leader Joseph Dendounga said he would meet Sergeant Anicet Saoulet, so-called coordinator of the rebel action. It was not clear when the meeting would be held.
Hospital sources said at least seven people, all civilians, had been killed since the start of the revolt on November 16.
Rebel sources reported casualties on the side of the presidential guard defending Patasse along with French troops who are based in the former colony under bilateral accords.
There was no independent or official confirmation of this.
Following clashes on Thursday and Friday, Patasse decreed a night curfew on Bangui on Saturday and repeated his call on mutineers to lay down their weapons unconditionally.
An uneasy calm reigned in the capital on Monday, a public holiday to mark National Day on Sunday. Shops, some of which were looted on Friday and Saturday, were closed.
Mutineers hold the main Kassai military barracks outside Bangui and the armoury there. Loyalists in Kassai have joined pro-Patasse forces in the Camp de Roux near the city centre.

Rebels have complete control of southern and western Bangui, notably around the Sixth Arrondisement. Outside the capital they hold sway in Lobaye barracks in the south and Boumbari and Bangassou near the eastern border with Zaire, home of Yakoma elements loyal to former president Andre Kolingba.
Soldiers have hardened long-running grievances over pay and status into political demands, which have split the army between troops from Patasse's northern region and those from the south.
Southerners are suspected of allegiance to Kolingba, who was defeated by Patasse in multiparty elections in 1993.

France reinforced its Bangui base after the mutiny started. But unlike their heavy intervention with helicopter gunships and armoured vehicles during a more serious revolt in May, the French appear to be avoiding clashes with rebels this time.
